name: SilverLining (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: cooling the planet, if research leads to its use, spares heat deaths everywhere, so the result is spread by world population, as for every tonne of CO₂ kept out of the air.
summary: SilverLining (Washington, DC) funds and coordinates research on solar radiation modification (cooling the planet by reflecting a little sunlight) and works with governments and others on how it is researched and governed; this model values what it added to that field in 2019-2024: its own research grants and science, its engagement work and grants abroad, other funders' money it directed, and the US federal research line (NOAA's Earth's Radiation Budget, about $8M a year since 2020) its policy work helped start, against its spending over those years ($6.5M in 2024). A dollar of the field's work is worth a share of the heat deaths a use of cooling would avert, put into tonnes of CO₂ by how much a tonne warms: a 30% chance of a use this century, 0.6°C for 50 years, the field's work adding a tenth of its benefit by improving how it is used, over all the field's funding until then. At the defaults a dollar given averts the heat deaths of about 1.0 tonne of CO₂, about 0.12 years of healthy life per $1,000; it is more than ten times its peers because cooling acts on the warming itself, so the decision the field informs weighs hundreds of billions of tonnes, and the field is small (about $44M a year). Whether cooling is used at all is one event, so at the default risk setting the counted figure is near zero. The result is mostly uncertainty, resting on judgments no study settles (how much the field's work improves a use, whether there is one), and every branch is discounted for missing data.

rows.label: The line's yearly money counted as field work
Cooling if solar radiation modification is used, averaged over its years
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 0.6°C (0.2 to 1.2): the size of a use the research informs. Anchor: the most studied design, ARISE-SAI (Richter et al. 2022; SilverLining's grants and its chief scientist took part), starts injections in 2035 and holds warming at 1.5°C above pre-industrial under the intermediate scenario SSP2-4.5, which the IPCC puts at 2.0°C in 2041-2060 and 2.7°C in 2081-2100 (Table SPM.1): a cooling of about 0.5°C at mid-century rising to 1.2°C by its end. Lower if it is used only to shave a peak, or under lower emissions.

source.title: Richter et al. (2022), Assessing Responses and Impacts of Solar climate intervention on the Earth system with stratospheric aerosol injection (ARISE-SAI), Geoscientific Model Development 15, 8221
source.quote: keep global mean surface air temperature near 1.5 °C above the pre-industrial value

rows.label: Years solar radiation modification is used, if used
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 50 years (20 to 100): holding back warming while emissions fall and carbon is removed takes decades (ARISE's design runs to 2069 and its successors beyond); a short use ends early by choice or by a halt.

rows.label: Chance solar radiation modification is used at a climate-relevant scale this century
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 30% (10% to 60%): 66% of 120 IPCC-contributing researchers who answered a 2025 survey expect a large-scale deployment attempt this century; an attempt is not a sustained use of the size above, and respondents chose to answer, so the best guess is about half of it. A single event (normalization.md 2.18): cooling is used this century or it isn't, so at the default risk setting the counted figure is near zero, and above 70% the full payoff counts.

source.title: SRM360 (30 October 2025), Scientists expect an SRM deployment attempt this century (New Scientist survey)
source.quote: a similar proportion expect a large-scale deployment attempt this century

rows.label: Share of the cooling's benefit the field's work (research, governance, advocacy) adds through better decisions
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 10% (2% to 30%): the field's work does not cool the planet; it changes when and how cooling is used. Its value, in the worlds where cooling is used, is the difference between the use made with it and without it: a well-designed, governed use (injection sites and amounts that limit regional harms such as shifted monsoons, an end that avoids a sudden rebound) instead of a crude one. We count that as a share of the gross benefit of the use, and divide it by all the field's funding (research about half of it, awareness and advocacy a fifth), so it is the share all that work adds. Value in worlds where cooling is never used (a harmful use talked out of) is not counted. No study estimates it; the anchor is that without research a use would still be possible (it is cheap) but blind, and that survey respondents name unknown consequences as the main risk (80%, SRM360's summary of the 2025 survey).

rows.label: Years over which a tonne's heat deaths are counted
rows.explainer: From the emission year to the end of Rethink Priorities' count (2020-2300), the years over which the shared heat-death rate spreads a tonne's warming.

rows.label: Tonnes of CO₂ whose heat deaths the cooling would avert, if used
rows.explainer: Cooling × years ÷ (a tonne's warming × the years its heat deaths are counted): a cooling of 0.6°C for 50 years spares the heat deaths of about 240 billion tonnes, about six years of the world's emissions. It puts cooling into the site's tonnes so the shared conversion values it (normalization.md 2.5); only heat deaths, since cooling doesn't remove the air pollution of fuel.

rows.label: Funding for all solar radiation modification work, per year, 2021-2025
rows.explainer: Everyone's spending on the field each year (research 50%, awareness and advocacy 21%, the rest outdoor tests, governance and commercial work), philanthropic, government and commercial, SilverLining's own funders included. The range is ours: the tracker counts only transactions it knows of, and its own totals differ slightly between figures.

source.title: SRM360 (September 2026), Who funds work on solar geoengineering? (2026 funding tracker)
source.quote: only about $44 million per year in overall funding for SRM between 2021 and 2025

rows.label: Average yearly funding until a decision, as a multiple of 2021-2025's
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 2× (1× to 4×): funding grew more than tenfold in a decade (SRM360), and the UK's ARIA alone committed about $77M over several years; it may keep growing as warming passes 1.5°C, or stall as governments pull back (SRM360 notes other governments falling back).

rows.label: Years of the field's work that inform the decision
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 20 years (10 to 35): research from about 2020 until a decision to use it or not, which the 2025 survey's respondents and ARISE's 2035 start place in the 2030s to 2050s.

rows.label: All funding for the field until a decision
Tonnes a typical dollar of the field's work is worth
rows.explainer: The chance of use × the tonnes its heat deaths equal × the share the field's work adds, over all the field's funding until the decision: an average dollar of the field. SilverLining's dollars enter below at this value, with their own adjustments. At the defaults about 4 tonnes a dollar before the timing correction (×2.3, timing_adj) and any adjustment, about 11 cents a tonne after the correction, against $0.50-3.50 a tonne for the climate funds' best picks (facts: climate, top_climate_fund_usd_per_tco2e): cheaper because cooling would offset the warming of hundreds of billions of tonnes at once, and the field whose research shapes that decision spends about $44M a year. This is why the model is far above the climate median (its peers' tonnes are each a policy's emissions cut); after its adjustments (about $1 a tonne) it is near the climate funds' best picks.

rows.label: Probability the outcome happens because of this work
rows.explainer: 1 for the research, engagement and directed-money branches: the grants were made, the work done and the money directed in the period; the chances (of use, of the work mattering) are in the value of a field dollar above. The federal line takes the shared advocacy share instead (pol_p_success).

rows.label: Years the federal research line counts
rows.explainer: The site's one answer for a won reform (docs/normalization.md 2.9): the programme's yearly money counts for the years it came earlier than it would have.

rows.label: Years from the work until the heat deaths it averts start to count
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 0 (0 to 15): the deaths come while cooling is used, before a tonne's would (the shared conversion counts a tonne's heat deaths at its own delay), so there is no further wait beyond the decision itself (up to 2 years); when the use starts, early or late, is deaths_earlier_years' question, which corrects for how much sooner the deaths come than a tonne's.

rows.label: Years sooner the cooling's heat deaths come than a tonne's
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 21 years (6 to 29): the shared conversion discounts a tonne's heat deaths as if they all came 60 years after it is avoided, the discount-weighted middle of a flat stream of deaths over 2020-2300 at 4% (such a stream is worth 0.093 of deaths today, against 1.04^-60 = 0.095). A use of 50 years starting about 18 years after the period's middle (field_years_to_decision less the years already past) has its discount-weighted middle about 39.5 years out (the stream is worth 0.212 of deaths today): about 21 years sooner (the exact ratio, 2.23 at 4%, is matched within 5% at rates from 1% to 4%). Low end a use starting in the mid-2050s (about 6 years), high end one starting in the early 2030s (about 28). At lower discount rates the correction shrinks with the rate, as it should (its effect is (1 + rate) to this power).

rows.label: Correction for the cooling's heat deaths coming sooner than a tonne's
rows.explainer: The years sooner, at the shared discount rate: 2.3 at 4%, 1.2 at 1%, nearly 1 at 0.1%.

rows.label: Discount for the wait
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate; the unit's conversion then discounts the heat deaths, so nothing is discounted twice.

rows.label: Years the federal line counts, discounted
Years the federal line counts, discounted, after the wait
Its other policy results, as a share of the federal line's value
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 15% (5% to 50%): the White House's congressionally mandated research plan (2023), which it says its advocacy supported, and its other work with officials in the US and abroad. They shape the decisions the field's work informs, as the federal line does, but no money or rule follows from them. Research it funded that informed UN reports is in the research branch, and its engagement abroad in the engagement branch, so neither is counted here.

rows.label: All branches, before adjustments
Trust in the chain from research dollars to heat deaths
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 0.7 (0.4 to 1): cooling is not the reverse of a tonne: it cools the tropics more than the poles and changes rainfall, so heat deaths in the hot places where most of them happen may fall a little less than a tonne-for-tonne reckoning says; the share research adds is a guess with no study behind it. As for Project Drawdown's research (0.7).

rows.explainer: Our judgment, 60% (30% to 90%): the advocates' part of the win as a whole is the shared figure (pol_p_success); among advocates, it was one of only two organisations to disclose lobbying on solar geoengineering in the decade to 2023 (the other Carnegie Mellon University, in 2013: E&E News, 2 March 2023, 'Blocking sun rays finds support in the Senate'), and its director advised Rep. McNerney's office on his bill for a formal NOAA programme, introduced as the first money passed (MIT Technology Review). Other advocates: researchers who testified and wrote for it, and the National Academies' 2021 call for a federal programme.

rows.label: Side effect: atmospheric science that serves other uses, as a share of the modelled value
rows.explainer: Our judgment, +10% (+2% to +30%): measurements and models of aerosols and clouds it funded serve weather and climate science beyond cooling: the Hunga eruption balloon campaign, ship-plume measurements relevant to the warming from the 2020 cut in shipping's sulphur, and the stratospheric observations of the federal line.

rows.label: Side effect: less effort to cut emissions because cooling looks possible, as a share of the modelled value
rows.explainer: Our judgment, -3% (-15% to +2%): research that makes cooling look feasible could weaken the push to cut emissions; survey experiments find the effect small, and some find the opposite (people told of geoengineering support cuts more), so the range runs through zero.

rows.label: Side effect: a hasty or ungoverned use made likelier, as a share of the modelled value
rows.explainer: Our judgment, -8% (-30% to -1%): research and advocacy that make cooling familiar can make an early use by one country or a company likelier (a start-up released sulphur balloons in 2022; a venture-funded firm now develops a proprietary particle), with the harms research is meant to prevent. Small beside the value, since SilverLining backs open research and government oversight, and such actors don't depend on it.
